title: India's Gen Alpha Walks Out of Class, Demanding Schools That Actually Work
excerpt: Children across at least 10 Indian states are protesting crumbling school buildings, absent teachers and unsafe conditions, building on the Gen Z exam-leak movement that toppled an education minister.
body:
• School students across at least 10 Indian states have launched protests demanding basic infrastructure — buildings, teachers, drinking water, electricity and functioning toilets — in government-run schools.
  • The wave follows the Gen Z-led Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) movement that forced the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan over exam paper leaks in July 2026.
  • India operates 1.5 million schools serving 247 million students, but over 100,000 schools have only a single teacher across all grades, and nearly 2.9 million children attend them.
  • With more than 30 percent of India's population under 18, the protests carry political weight ahead of the 2029 national elections.

Children as young as six in rural India are doing something culturally rare: walking out of their classrooms in organized protest against the very institutions meant to educate them.

Since late July, students in at least 10 states — including Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Rajasthan, Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh and Jharkhand — have staged demonstrations outside schools, marched to government offices and blocked roads demanding basic facilities that India's Right to Education Act has guaranteed since 2009.

Where It Started

In the village of Samuhi Bhatpurwa in Uttar Pradesh, 122 primary school students refused to enter their classrooms until authorities promised to rebuild their dilapidated school building. A wall had collapsed on a student in 2023, causing severe injuries, and repairs were never made.

"The fear does not let us concentrate on our studies. That is why we all protested," an eight-year-old student told Al Jazeera. A block education officer visited the school and promised a new building would be constructed.

Similar scenes unfolded across the country. In Bihar's Simuara village, around 50 students walked four kilometres to meet a senior bureaucrat, complaining about substandard midday meals prepared with unwashed ingredients and a broken water pump. In Lucknow, hundreds of schoolgirls blocked a major road demanding teachers and improved hostel facilities. In Rajasthan's Alwar, students launched an indefinite protest after a school building slab collapsed.

From Gen Z to Gen Alpha

The school protests follow directly from the Gen Z youth movement that swept India this summer. Starting in June, thousands of young people converged on Jantar Mantar in New Delhi, demanding accountability over a series of high-profile examination paper leaks linked to dozens of student suicides.

The movement was spearheaded by the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP), a satirical organization formed in May 2026. After security forces cracked down on peaceful marchers heading toward parliament, the protests drew wider national support and forced the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan in late July.

"The children are demanding their rights. They want teachers, benches, school buildings, drinking water, electricity and toilets. Unfortunately, for a long time, the basic infrastructure and manpower to run schools have been missing."

— Nagasimha Rao, education rights activist

The CJP has since pivoted to a grassroots campaign called "School Thik Karo" (Fix the Schools), launched on India's Independence Day on August 15. CJP members have begun visiting schools across states to document conditions and support student-led protests.

The Scale of the Crisis

India operates one of the world's largest education systems — 1.5 million schools serving 247 million students. While government data shows improving teacher-pupil ratios and declining dropout rates, the numbers mask deep disparities.

Official figures show 100,843 government schools have only a single teacher for all grades, with 2.9 million children enrolled in them. India also has 5,663 "ghost schools" — institutions with no students at all. The crisis disproportionately affects children from economically and socially marginalized communities who attend government-run schools.

What It Means for the Diaspora

For the Indian diaspora, the protests highlight the widening gulf between India's ambitions as a global education power and the reality in its government schools. Many NRI families maintain connections to rural India and fund schools or charities in their home villages. The Gen Alpha movement raises pointed questions about whether those investments and India's National Education Policy 2020 are translating into real outcomes on the ground.

"These children are tomorrow's voters too. They will definitely vote keeping in mind the interest of the country's education system."

— Akash Sarkar, education activist

What's Next

With more than 30 percent of India's population under 18, many of the children joining protests today will be eligible voters by the 2029 national elections. Educationist Swarna Rajagopalan has called for systemic reforms including equal infrastructure everywhere, better teacher recruitment and stronger measures to keep children in school. Whether the Modi government responds with structural change or temporary assurances will determine if this movement fades or intensifies.
